details:
**Carmen (Georges Bizet)**
The most famous French opera, about a Gypsy cigarette-factory worker in Seville. Carmen sings the "Habanera," calling love a "rebellious bird" ("L'amour est un oiseau rebelle"), dances a seguidilla after her arrest by Lieutenant Zuniga, seduces the soldier Don José, and is stabbed by him after she turns to the toreador Escamillo.

**The Pearl Fishers and other French operas**
Bizet's The Pearl Fishers contains the "friendship duet" "Au fond du temple saint," in which Nadir and Zurga recall seeing a woman in a temple. Other famous French opera excerpts include the "Flower Duet" sung by Lakmé and her servant by a river in Léo Delibes's Lakmé, and the violin "Méditation" from Jules Massenet's Thaïs.

**War of the Buffoons (Querelle des Bouffons)**
A 1750s Parisian pamphlet war between supporters of France's serious operatic "musical tragedy" (tragédie lyrique) and supporters of Italian comic opera buffa, sparked by performances of Pergolesi's La serva padrona. Jean-Philippe Rameau came under fire as the leading representative of the French style.

**Jean-Baptiste Lully**
The Italian-born court composer to Louis XIV who dominated French Baroque music and pioneered the comédie-ballet with Molière and choreographer Pierre Beauchamp. He is credited with the "French overture" (a slow section with dotted rhythms followed by a fast fugal section), and he died of gangrene after striking his foot with the long staff he used to beat time.

**Jean-Philippe Rameau**
A French Baroque composer and theorist whose 1722 Treatise on Harmony controversially grounded harmony in mathematical and acoustic principles. His operas include the tragédie lyrique Hippolyte et Aricie and the opéra-ballet Les Indes galantes, whose exotic acts include one set among Peruvian Incas and the "Dance of the Peace Pipe."

**François Couperin**
A French Baroque harpsichordist nicknamed "le Grand," who wrote the treatise The Art of Playing the Harpsichord (L'art de toucher le clavecin) and the harpsichord piece "Les Barricades mystérieuses," written in the arpeggiated French "broken style" (style brisé). Maurice Ravel honored him with the six-movement suite Le Tombeau de Couperin.

**Boléro (Maurice Ravel)**
A ballet score commissioned by dancer Ida Rubinstein, built on a single snare drum rhythm repeated 169 times beneath a slow crescendo. Ravel's other works include a G major piano concerto that opens with a whip crack and a Piano Concerto for the Left Hand commissioned by Paul Wittgenstein.

**Pavane for a Dead Princess and Gabriel Fauré**
Ravel's Pavane, dedicated to the Princesse de Polignac, was written while he studied at the Paris Conservatoire under Gabriel Fauré, who had written his own Pavane in F-sharp minor. Fauré's cello and piano pieces include the Élégie, the Sicilienne, and "Papillon," depicting a butterfly's flight.

**The Rite of Spring riot and other Paris ballet premieres**
Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring caused a riot at its 1913 premiere at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, where Camille Saint-Saëns supposedly said "If that's a bassoon, I'm a baboon." Other notable French ballets include Adolphe Adam's Giselle, whose title role, premiered by Carlotta Grisi, joins the ghostly Wilis, and Erik Satie's scandalous Parade, with designs by Pablo Picasso and a score using a typewriter and sirens.

**French New Wave cinema**
A 1950s–60s film movement led by François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard. Truffaut's The 400 Blows follows Antoine Doinel, who is accused of plagiarizing Balzac and ends running to the ocean; Godard's Breathless, about a car thief who idolizes Humphrey Bogart, is famous for its jump cuts.

**Henri Cartier-Bresson and the "decisive moment"**
A French photojournalist whose idea of the "decisive moment" is exemplified by his 1932 photograph of a man leaping over a puddle behind the Gare Saint-Lazare in Paris. Other well-known images show a blurred cyclist seen from the top of a staircase in Hyères and a crowd at a Shanghai bank buying gold.

**Louis Daguerre and early French photography**
Daguerre invented the daguerreotype, the first commercial photographic process, using iodized silver plates, and his view of a Paris boulevard is the first photograph to show a person (a man having his shoes shined). Nicéphore Niépce took the oldest surviving photograph from a window in France, the photographer Nadar was caricatured by Honoré Daumier in a balloon "elevating photography to the height of art," and the Lumière brothers patented the Autochrome color process.

**Olivier Messiaen**
A French composer who wrote Quartet for the End of Time as a prisoner of war, with movements like "Crystal Liturgy" and "Abyss of the Birds" reflecting his love of birdsong. He also wrote the Turangalîla-Symphonie, whose title comes from two Sanskrit words, and described his "modes of limited transposition" in The Technique of My Musical Language.

**Erik Satie and Pierre Boulez**
Satie wrote the slow piano dances Gymnopédies (named for an ancient Greek festival), the Gnossiennes, the piece Vexations (a short theme to be repeated 840 times), and "furniture music." Boulez, a leading postwar modernist, wrote Le Marteau sans maître ("The Hammer without a Master") and founded the Paris electronic music institute IRCAM.

**Henri Matisse and Fauvism**
The leader of the Fauves ("wild beasts"), a name critic Louis Vauxcelles gave the group at the 1905 Salon d'Automne in Paris. Matisse's works include a portrait of his wife with a green stripe down her face, The Red Room (Harmony in Red), and The Joy of Life and The Dance, which show circles of dancers.
